## Introduction

This interactive tutorial will guide you through common **dplyr**, **ggplot2** and base R functions for data manipulation.
You will practice with real data sets like `mtcars`, `iris`, `starwars`, and `airquality`.

### About this tutorial

These exercises are meant to be complementary to the *Digital Research Toolkit for Linguists* offered in the summer semester 2025 at the University of Stuttgart.
I reference the materials and examples from the seminar in several places.
The relevant slides and exercises are available from the GitHub repository: [LINK](https://github.com/a-nap/Digital-Research-Toolkit).

For questions and feedback, please contact Anna Prysłopska at `anna . pryslopska [AT] gmail . com`

Topics covered include:

1.  Navigating working directories and file structure
2.  Installing, loading, and unloading R packages
3.  Previewing and exploring data
4.  Data preprocessing:
    -   Selecting and renaming columns
    -   Filtering values (with an introduction to set theory)
    -   Handling missing values
    -   Creating new variables
    -   Sorting rows
    -   Identifying unique values
5.  Grouping data and summarizing results
6.  Using conditional logic with if-else statements
7.  Assigning values and data input
8.  Creating dataframes, binding rows and columns
9.  Combining data with joins and merges
10. Visualizing data 

#### How to use this tutorial

This tutorial consists primarily of exercises. 
You will read a short description of the task and see a code chunk window, like the one below. 

```{r intro, exercise=TRUE}
# There is some code here
print("Hello world!")
```

```{r intro-solution}
# You can copy this code and it will print "Hello world!" 
print("Hello world!")
```

You write your solution in the code window and run it by pressing `shift`+`enter`.The result should appear below the exercise window.

Unfortunately, the run code button is disabled at the beginning for some reason (probably an error in the package or insufficient memory). 

If you get stuck, you can click on the *Hint* and/or *Solution* button to (incrementally) reveal the solution. You can then copy and paste the solution into the code window. Click on the *Hint* or *Solution* button again to close the popup window and return to the code chunk.

Your solution is not actually graded in this tutorial, so it does not look to see if your answer matches the solution. Rather, it's a guideline for self-study.

#### The tidyverse

In class, we used tidyverse functions over base R.
The [tidyverse](https://www.tidyverse.org/)  is a curated set of R packages tailored for data science, all built around a consistent design philosophy, shared grammar, and common structures.
They usually have punny names.

There is SO MUCH more to both the packages we used in class and the tidyverse overall. 

#### `dplyr`

[`dplyr`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/) is an R package in the tidyverse. It helps you work with data by providing you a set of simple, consistent commands that make it easier to do common tasks like filtering, sorting, and summarizing data.

#### `ggplot2`

I class, we have been using the `ggplot2` and `esquisse` packages to visualize data. In this tutorial, you will practice plotting with the former package.

[`ggplot2`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/) is a tool for making graphs. Its approach to data viz is that of a layered grammar of graphics. You design and construct graphics in
a structured manner from data upwards.
First, you tell it what data to use, how to match data to things like color or position, and what kind of shapes to draw (like bars or lines). Then `ggplot2` builds the graph for you, handling the rest of the work.

`ggplot2` was created by Hadley Wickham.  

![Diagram from slides in Week 7](https://pryslopska.com/img/ggplot2025.svg){width="50%"}

#### `esquisse`

[`esquisse`](https://dreamrs.github.io/esquisse/) is a package that lets you explore data interactively in a graphical user interface. It uses `ggplot2` for visualization.
You can export the generated graph and save the code to generate it.
It has its limitations but is useful to get a first impression/overview.

#### `mtcars`

The **`mtcars`** data set contains car data with fuel consumption and design specs for 32 car models taken from the US magazine *Motor Trend* (1973–74).

| Column | Explanation                              |
|--------|------------------------------------------|
| `mpg`  | Miles/(US) gallon                        |
| `cyl`  | Number of cylinders                      |
| `disp` | Displacement (cu.in.)                    |
| `hp`   | Gross horsepower                         |
| `drat` | Rear axle ratio                          |
| `wt`   | Weight (1000 lbs)                        |
| `qsec` | 1/4 mile time                            |
| `vs`   | Engine (0 = V-shaped, 1 = straight)      |
| `am`   | Transmission (0 = automatic, 1 = manual) |
| `gear` | Number of forward gears                  |

#### `iris` data set

The **`iris`** data set contains measurements (sepal/petal) of 150 iris flowers across three species.
Originally published by [the UCI Machine Learning Repository](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/data set/53/iris).

| Column         | Explanation      |
|----------------|------------------|
| `Sepal.Length` | Length of sepals |
| `Sepal.Width`  | Width of sepals  |
| `Petal.Length` | Length of petals |
| `Petal.Width`  | Width of petals  |
| `Species`      | One of 3 species |

![Flower diagram from Wikipedia](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7f/Mature_flower_diagram.svg){width="90%"}

#### `starwars` data set

The **`starwars`** data set from the `dplyr` package contains [data on characters from the Star Wars universe](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/starwars.html).

| Column | Explanation |
|----|----|
| `name` | Name of the character |
| `height` | Height (cm) |
| `mass` | Weight (kg) |
| `hair_color`, `skin_color`, `eye_color` | Hair, skin, and eye colors |
| `birth_year` | Year born (BBY = Before Battle of Yavin) |
| `sex` | The biological sex of the character, namely male, female, hermaphroditic, or none (as in the case for Droids). |
| `gender` | The gender role or gender identity of the character as determined by their personality or the way they were programmed (as in the case for Droids). |
| `homeworld` | Name of homeworld |
| `species` | Name of species |
| `films` | List of films the character appeared in |
| `vehicles` | List of vehicles the character has piloted |
| `starships` | List of starships the character has piloted |

#### `airquality` data set

The **`airquality`** data contains daily air quality measurements in New York (May–September 1973).

| Column | Explanation |
|----|----|
| `Ozone` | Mean ozone in parts per billion from 1300 to 1500 hours at Roosevelt Island |
| `Solar.R` | Solar radiation in Langleys in the frequency band 4000–7700 Angstroms from 0800 to 1200 hours at Central Park |
| `Wind` | Average wind speed in miles per hour at 0700 and 1000 hours at LaGuardia Airport |
| `Temp` | Maximum daily temperature in degrees Fahrenheit at La Guardia Airport. |

## 1. Working directory

*2 exercises*

A **directory** or **folder** is a container for storing files or other folders.
**File structure** or **file hierarchy** or **folder organization** is the way these containers are organized.

The working directory is where R will look for files, where R will save visible and hidden files, and where R will automatically load files from.

![File structure](https://pryslopska.com/img/filestructure.png){width="50%"}

## 4. `select()`

*4 exercises*

During data clean up, we selected only those columns that were meaningful for our analysis by using the function `select()`. All the other columns were removed.

You can use `select()` with operators to select variables, as per the documentation:

- `:` for selecting a range of consecutive variables.
- `!` for taking the complement of a set of variables.
- `&` and `|` for selecting the intersection or the union of two sets of variables.
- `c()` for combining selections.

### Exercise 4.1: Select specific columns

Use `select()` on `mtcars` data to choose miles per gallon, horse power, and weight columns.

```{r select-ex1, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r select-ex1-hint-1}
# The data is the first argument you must give to the function
```


```{r select-ex1-hint-2}
# The columns you need are: mpg, hp, wt
```

```{r select-ex1-solution}
select(mtcars, mpg, hp, wt)
```


```{r select-ex2-solution}

```




*3 exercises*

Sometimes, columns are named in a annoying or misleading way.


```{r rename-ex1-hint}

```

```{r rename-ex1-solution}

```

### Exercise 5.2: Rename multiple columns

In `starwars`, rename "birth_year" to "age" and "mass" to "weight."

```{r rename-ex2, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r rename-ex2-hint-1}
# You can simply list the new columns as arguments (comma separated) or use concatenation.
```



### Exercise 5.3: Rename after select

Select "species" and "homeworld" from `starwars` and rename them to "type" and "planet".

```{r rename-ex3, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r rename-ex3-hint-1}

```

```{r rename-ex3-hint-2}
# Rename the columns
# Remember to pass the correct variable to the second function.
df2 <- rename(df, 
              new1 = old1, 
              new2 = old2)
```

```{r rename-ex3-solution}
df1 <- select(starwars, species, homeworld)
df2 <- rename(df1, type = species, planet = homeworld)
```

## 6. `filter()`

*7 exercises*

Filtering rows is analogous to selecting columns.
Some rows are not relevant to us (or maybe at all!) and removing them makes it easier to determine the important information.

In class, we spoke about using R as a calculator and how it can do basic functions:

| Function                               | Symbol              |
|:---------------------------------------|---------------------|
| addition                               | `+`                 |
| subtraction                            | `-`                 |
| division                               | `/`                 |
| multiplication                         | `*`                 |
| power                                  | `^`                 |
| equals                                 | `==`                |
| does not equal                         | `!=`                |
| greater than                           | `>`                 |
| greater than or equal                  | `>=`                |
| less than                              | `<`                 |
| less than or equal                     | `<=`                |
| range (from NR1 to NR2)                | NR1`:`NR2           |
| identify element (is VALUE in OBJECT?) | VALUE `%in%` OBJECT |

We also practiced set theory.
**Set theory** is a part of math and a way to thinking about groups of things and how they relate to each other.
These "things" can be anything: numbers, letters, shapes, people, concepts, ideas, etc.
We call these collections sets and each thing inside the set is called an **element**.
Sets are useful because they allow us to analyze arguments using logic and structure, define categories (e.g. all living beings) and compare them ("some living beings are humans").
You can combine and compare sets by using unions ('or' `|`, so everything in A or B) and intersections ('and' `&`, so only what is in *both* A and B).

![Venn diagram from slides in Week 4](https://pryslopska.com/img/venn-logic.png){width="50%"}

### Exercise 6.1: Basic filtering

Filter `mtcars` for rows where the miles per gallon are more than 25.

```{r filter-ex1, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r filter-ex1-hint}
# Substitute "condition" for a statement that evaluates to TRUE
# In this case, miles per gallon is over 25.
filter(df, condition)
```

```{r filter-ex1-solution}

```

### Exercise 6.2: Multiple conditions

From `starwars`, keep only masculine characters which are taller than 180.

```{r filter-ex2, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r filter-ex2-hint-1}
# Option 1:
filter(df, 
       condition1, 
       condition2)
```

```{r filter-ex2-hint-2}
# Option 2:
filter(df, 
       condition1 & condition2)
```

```{r filter-ex2-solution}
# Option 1:
filter(starwars, 
       gender == 'masculine',
       height > 180)
# Option 2:
filter(starwars,
       gender == 'masculine' &
       height > 180)
```

### Exercise 6.3: Filter with %in%

On `iris`, filter only the setosa and versicolor species.

```{r filter-ex3, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r filter-ex3-hint}
# There are multiple ways to solve this exercise:
# Option 1: Using %in%
# Option 2: Using == and |
# Option 3: Using !=
```

```{r filter-ex3-solution}
# Option 1:
filter(iris, Species %in% c('setosa', 'versicolor'))
# Option 2:
filter(iris, Species == 'setosa' | Species == 'versicolor')
# Option 3:
filter(iris, Species != 'virginica')
```

### Exercise 6.4: More filters

On `iris`, how many flowers of the virginica species have the petal width of at least 2.5 and petal length of 6 or less?

```{r filter-ex4, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r filter-ex4-hint-1}
# As a reminder, you can combine the conditions in two ways:
# Option 1: As a comma-separated list
# Option 2: By using &
```

```{r filter-ex4-hint-2}
# Option 1:
filter(df, 
       condition1,
       condition2,
       cobndition3)
```

```{r filter-ex4-hint-3}
# Option 2:
filter(df, 
       condition1 & 
       condition2 &
       condition3)
```


```{r filter-ex4-solution}
# This is true of only 2 flowers
# Option 1:
filter(iris, 
       Species == 'virginica',
       Petal.Width > 2.4,
       Petal.Length <= 6.0)
# Option 2:
filter(iris, 
       Species == 'virginica' &
       Petal.Width > 2.4 &
       Petal.Length <= 6.0)
```

### Exercise 6.5: Mixing filters

Look at the `starwars` data.
What is the name and species of the man who is between 100 and 180 cm tall, has black or blue eyes, weighs 80 kg or less, does not have black hair, and whose homeworld is neither Sullust nor Bespin.

```{r filter-ex5, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r filter-ex5-hint-1}
# Build your filter incrementally
filter(starwars,
       sex == "male",
       height %in% 100:180)
```

```{r filter-ex5-hint-2}
# Again, there are many ways to achieve the same filter.
filter(starwars,
       sex == "male",
       height %in% 100:180,
       eye_color %in% c("black", "blue"))
```

```{r filter-ex5-hint-3}
# The conditions must evaluate to TRUE.
# One more is missing.
filter(starwars,
       sex == "male",
       height %in% 100:180,
       eye_color %in% c("black", "blue"),
       mass <= 80,
       hair_color != "black")
```

```{r filter-ex5-solution}
filter(starwars,
       sex == "male",
       height %in% 100:180,
       eye_color %in% c("black", "blue"),
       mass <= 80,
       hair_color != "black",
       !(homeworld %in% c("Sullust", "Bespin")))
```

<div>

<i class="fa-solid fa-circle-info"></i> **Hint:** You don't need to select the name and species.
It's enough if you return the row with this individual.

</div>

### Exercise 6.6: More mixing filters

Look at the `starwars` data.
What is the homeworld of the grey or green-skinned, bald man, who has neither yellow nor gold eyes.
They weigh under 90 kg and don't pilot the Millennium Falcon.
They're either over 230 cm or under 200 cm tall.

```{r filter-ex6, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r filter-ex6-hint-1}
# Start with the easy filters
filter(starwars,
       skin_color %in% c("grey", "green"),
       hair_color == "none",
       sex =="male",
       mass < 90,
       starships != "Millennium Falcon")
```

```{r filter-ex6-hint-2}
# As before, feel free to experiment with different ways to get the same result
filter(starwars,
       !(eye_color %in% c("yellow", "gold")))
```

```{r filter-ex6-hint-3}
# The last condition must evaluate to TRUE
filter(starwars,
       (height < 200 | height > 230))
```

```{r filter-ex6-solution}
# The solution as it is spelled out in the text
filter(starwars,
       skin_color %in% c("grey", "green"),
       hair_color == "none",
       sex =="male",
       !(eye_color %in% c("yellow", "gold")),
       mass < 90,
       starships != "Millennium Falcon",
       (height < 200 | height > 230))
```

<div>

<i class="fa-solid fa-circle-info"></i> **Hint:** You don't need to select the homeworld.
It's enough if you return the row with this individual.

</div>

### Exercise 6.7: Even more filters

Look at the `starwars` data.
Find the only woman with a combined height and mass under 200.

```{r filter-ex7, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r filter-ex7-solution}
filter(starwars,
       sex =="female",
       (height + mass) < 200)
```

## 7. `mutate()`

*3 exercises*

In R, mutating means adding new columns or changing existing ones in a dataframe.

### Exercise 7.1: Create a new column

In `mtcars`, make a new column called "power_to_weight" which is the ratio of horse power to weight.

```{r mutate-ex1, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here


```

```{r mutate-ex1-hint}
# This is the general function syntax
mutate(df, new_column = value)
```

```{r mutate-ex1-solution}
mutate(mtcars, power_to_weight = hp / wt)
```

<div>

<i class="fa-solid fa-circle-info"></i> **Hint:** To calculate the ratio you need to divide one thing by the other.
Check the column names in the code window or in the introduction to figure out which values you need.

</div>

### Exercise 7.2: Multiple mutations

In `starwars`, calculate two values:

-   "height_m" each character's height in meters, and
-   "bmi" [the body mass index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_mass_index) of each character.

$$
\text{BMI} = \frac{\text{weight (kg)}}{[\text{height (m)}]^2}
$$


**Don't use pipes for this exercise.**

```{r mutate-ex2, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```


## 8. `na.omit()`

*7 exercises*

There are many ways in which you can deal with missing values, which is what R calls `NA`.
You can remove them (which is what we're doing here), set them to a specific value, or other things.
In class, we simply removed all NAs.
As a rule of thumb, you want to look at what values are missing from your data to see if there is anything amiss with it.

This function takes only one argument.

## 9. `arrange()`

*4 exercises*

This function is used to sort the values in a dataframe.
By default, `arrange()` sorts the values in ascending order (smallest to largest or alphabetically from A to Z). 
You can use the function `desc()` on a column name from **within** `arrange()` to sort values in descending order.
If the values in a column are numerical, you can also inverse the sorting order by using `-` in front of the column name.

The values are sorted first by the first column, then by the second, then by the third and so on.

### Exercise 9.1: Ascending order

Arrange `mtcars` by weight and horsepower, both in ascending order.

```{r arrange-ex1-solution}

```

```{r arrange-ex2-hint}
# Option 2:
arrange(df, desc(column))
```

```{r arrange-ex2-solution}
# Option 1:

# Option 2:
arrange(starwars, desc(height))
```

## 11. Pipes

*7 exercises*

A powerful tool for clearly expressing a sequence of multiple operations.
Passes the output as the new input.
They can be read as "and then".

The pipe translates `x |> f(y)` into `f(x, y)`.

```{r pipe-ex1-hint}
# You must skip the first argument of select()
```

```{r pipe-ex1-solution}

```

## 12. Grouping and summarizing

*8 + 2 exercises*

When you group data with `group_by()`, you're putting it into categories based on one or more columns (like grouping people by age or cars by number of cylinders).
Calling the grouping function does not change anything *visibly* but it changes the data "under the hood".

When you summarize with `summarize()`, you calculate some new values for each group—like the average, total, or count.
`summarize()` calculates a single value (per group) and drops columns which are not grouped by.
In contrast, `mutate()` changes an existing column or adds a new one, but does not drop columns.

**Use pipes to solve these exercises.**

Recall that in Week 3 of the course we talked about the measures of central tendency (mean, median, standard deviation etc.).
If you get stuck on these exercises, check the handout for week 3, pages 22-24.

### Exercise 12.1: Average

Group `mtcars` by number of cylinders and compute average miles per gallon.

```{r group-ex1, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r group-ex1-solution}
mtcars |>
  group_by(cyl) |>
  summarise(avg_mpg = mean(mpg))
```

<div>

<i class="fa-solid fa-circle-info"></i> **Hint:** Use `mean()` to calculate the mean value.

</div>

## 13. If else statements

*8 exercises*

In class, we used `ifelse()` and `case_when()` to recode values for conditions and also validate the answers to the Moses illusion questions.

-   Use `ifelse()` when you have one condition (or maybe two). It’s great for simple either/or decisions.
-   Use `case_when()` when you have multiple conditions. It checks several conditions in order, and returns the first one that's true.

**Remember to use pipes to solve these exercises.**

![Diagram of an if else statement](https://pryslopska.com/img/ifelse.png){width="50%"}

### Exercise 13.1: Flag efficient cars

Create a new column called "efficient" in which you flag `mtcars` cars with mpg \> 20 as efficient.

```{r ifelse-ex1, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r ifelse-ex1-solution}
mtcars |>
  mutate(efficient = ifelse(mpg > 20, 'Yes', "No"))
```

### Exercise 13.2: Label engine size

Create a column "size" labeling engines as "Large" or "Small" based on displacement with a threshold of 200.

```{r ifelse-ex2, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r ifelse-ex2-solution}
mtcars |>
  mutate(size = ifelse(disp > 200, 'Large', 'Small'))
```

### Exercise 13.3: Case when for speed class

Label the cars in `mtcars` with a speed class based on horse power: "High" for over 150 horse power, "Medium" for over 100 horse power, and "Low" otherwise.
Use `case_when()`, because you have 3 options.

```{r casewhen-ex3, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r casewhen-ex3-solution}
mtcars |>
  mutate(speed_class = case_when(hp > 150 ~ 'High',
                                 hp > 100 ~ 'Medium',
                                 TRUE ~ 'Low'))
```

<div>

**Hint:** `TRUE` is the final "else" statement.

</div>

### Exercise 13.4: Categorize characters by height

Categorize characters by height in `starwars`: "Very tall" for 200 cm or more, "Tall" for over 180 cm, "Medium" for 150 cm or more, and "Small" for under 150 cm.
Show only the name, height, and height class.


```{r casewhen-ex4-solution}
                                  height > 180 ~ 'Tall',
                                  height >= 150 ~ 'Medium',

  select(name, height, height_class)
```

</div>

### Exercise 13.6: Label temperature levels

Label `airquality` days as "Hot", "Warm", or "Cool" based on temperature in °Celsius.

```{r casewhen-ex6, exercise=TRUE, hint="Use Temp thresholds in case_when()."}
# Write your code here

```

```{r casewhen-ex6-solution}
airquality |>
  mutate(
    Temp_C = (Temp - 32) * 5/9,
    Temp_Label = case_when(
      Temp_C >= 30 ~ "Hot",
      Temp_C >= 20 ~ "Warm",
      TRUE         ~ "Cool"
    )
  )
```

### Exercise 13.7: Case when for iris petal size

Classify `iris` flowers by petal length using `case_when()`: "small", "medium", "large".
Base your classification on the quantiles.

```{r casewhen-ex7, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r casewhen-ex7-solution}
iris |>
  mutate(
```

### Exercise 13.8: Engine performance tier

Add column to `mtcars`: "Economy" (horse power under 100 and more than 25 miles per gallon), "Balanced" (between 100 and 200 horse power and at least 15 miles per gallon), "Performance" (more than 200 horse power) tiers.
Any remaining cars should be classified as "Other".
Lastly, count how many cars are in each of these classes.

```{r casewhen-ex8, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r casewhen-ex8-solution}
mtcars |>
  mutate(
    Tier = case_when(
      hp < 100 & mpg > 25 ~ "Economy",
      hp >= 100 & hp <= 200 & mpg >= 15 ~ "Balanced",
      hp > 200 ~ "Performance",
      TRUE ~ "Other")
    ) |>
  group_by(Tier) |>
  summarise(Count = n())
```

<div>

**Hint:** Remember how we combined conditions when filtering and in set theory.

</div>

## 14. Assignment and data input

In R, you can use three operators to assign values to a variable: `->`, `=`, and `->>`.

| Operator | Example | Uses |
|----|----|----|
| `<-` and `->` | `x <- 5` | This is the traditional way of assigning values. You can read it as "Put 5 in x". |
| `=` | `x = 5` | This is similar to the operator above. It works fine in most cases and is usually used inside functions (like `nrow(x = starwars)`). You can read the example as "Set x equal to 5". |
| `->>` and `<<-` | `x <<- 5` | This is a special kind of `<-` operator: a "global assignment" operator. It assigns 5 to x in the **global environment** (outside the local scope), even if you're inside a function. In lay terms, it makes the variable jump out of its environment and become global. |

In this course, we use the `->` operator for assigning global values (e.g. outside of functions) and the `=` operator for assigning values inside functions.

```{r, echo=FALSE, include=TRUE}
starwars_rows <- nrow(x = starwars)
```

### Exercise 15.4: Combining data with `cbind()`

Think of `cbind()` as adding more columns to your data.
Use it when you're adding new types of information about your existing entries (like currency and timezone).
It is used to bind any number of dataframes by column.
The resulting dataframe is wider.

| Egypt     | Cairo    | Africa        | 118.084    | Arabic             |
| Germany   | Berlin   | Europe        | 84.145     | German             |
| Australia | Canberra | Oceania       | 26.934     | English            |

```{r crbind1, exercise=TRUE}
timezone    <- c(

  "UTC+09:00", # Japan (Tokyo)
  "UTC-03:00", # Brazil (Brasília)
  "UTC+02:00", # Egypt (Cairo)
```

```{r crbind1-solution, exercise=TRUE}
# Adding the four new countries.

                        kenya,

                        Timezone = timezone,
                        Calling_code = calling_code)


countries_final <- arrange(countries_data,
                          Continent,
                          -Population,
                          Timezone)
countries_final
```

## 16. Joining data

*10 exercises*

Sometimes, you have two dataframes, and you want to combine them based on something they have in common (e.g. matching people by name, countries by continent, or books by title and author).
`merge()` is a built-in R function.
It looks for a common column (like "Country") in two dataframes and joins the rows that match.
The `dplyr` package gives you more precise control with functions like:

-   `left_join()`
-   `right_join()`
-   `inner_join()`
-   `full_join()`
-   `anti_join()`

They all do the same basic thing as `merge()`: combine two dataframes using a shared column.
But they let you choose what to keep if there's not a perfect match.

![Venn diagram from slides in Week 5](https://pryslopska.com/img/venn-join.png){width="50%"}

### Exercise 16.1: Full join two small dataframes

For this exercise, do the following tasks:

1.  Create a dataframe with names of 10 children **in this order** (Lila, Kai, Ezra, Maya, Ethan, Zoe, Leo, Isla, Raja, Zara) and their ages (7, 2, 12, 4, 3, 2, 10, 13, 6, 7), assign it to `children`.
2.  Create a second dataframe with the names of the children **in this order** (Zoe, Kai, Lila, Ethan, Leo, Ezra, Isla, Zara, Maya, Raja) and their favorite animals (Clownfish, Panda, Elephant, Penguin, Koala, Tiger, Giraffe, Rabbit, Cat, Fox), assign it to `animals`.
3.  Use `full_join()` to join these two dataframes by the common identifier column.

```{r joinpractice-ex1, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```

```{r joinpractice-ex1-solution}
children <- data.frame(
  Name = c("Lila", "Kai", "Ezra", "Maya", "Ethan", "Zoe", "Leo", "Isla", "Raja", "Zara"),
  Age = c(7, 2, 12, 4, 3, 2, 10, 13, 6, 7))

animals <- data.frame(
  Name = c("Zoe", "Kai", "Lila", "Ethan", "Leo", "Ezra", "Isla", "Zara", "Maya", "Raja"),
  Animal = c("Clownfish", "Panda", "Elephant", "Penguin", "Koala", "Tiger", "Giraffe", "Rabbit", "Cat", "Fox"))

full_join(children, animals, by="Name")
```

<div>

**Hint:** The `full_join()` function takes as argument two dataframes and the common identifier arguments by which to match the rows `by=`.

</div>

### Exercise 16.8: Add missing ages and schools

When using `full_join()` on the `children` and `animals` dataframes, there were ages missing from a few kids.
In this exercise you will:

1.  Create a dataframe for children and their favorite animals (this code is provided for you).
2.  Use `full_join()` to create a combined dataframe of `children` and `animals`.
3.  Using `case_when()`, add the ages for Catherine (5), Takeshi and Sven (both 8), Anouk (3), and Amara (11).
4.  Then, create a new column called `School` for the school they go to:
    -   1-5: Preschool
    -   6-9: Primary school
    -   10-15: Middle school
    -   16+: High school
5.  Calculate the number of children (`N`) and their average age (`Mean_age`) per school.
6.  Sort the results by number of children.
7.  Print the resulting dataframe.

**Use pipes to complete steps 2-7.**

```{r joinpractice-ex8, exercise=TRUE}
children <- data.frame(
  Name = c("Lila", "Kai", "Ezra", "Maya", "Ethan", "Zoe", "Leo", "Isla", "Raja", "Zara"),
  Age = c(7, 2, 12, 4, 3, 2, 10, 13, 6, 7))

animals <- data.frame(
  Name = c("Zoe", "Kai", "Lila", "Ethan", "Leo", "Ezra", "Isla", "Zara", "Maya", "Raja", "Catherine", "Takeshi", "Sven", "Anouk", "Amara"),
  Animal = c("Clownfish", "Panda", "Elephant", "Penguin", "Koala", "Tiger", "Giraffe", "Rabbit", "Cat", "Fox", "Dog", "Otter", "Parrot", "Owl", "Llama"))

###################################
# Start your code here
###################################


```

```{r joinpractice-ex8-solution}
children <- data.frame(
  Name = c("Lila", "Kai", "Ezra", "Maya", "Ethan", "Zoe", "Leo", "Isla", "Raja", "Zara"),
  Age = c(7, 2, 12, 4, 3, 2, 10, 13, 6, 7))

animals <- data.frame(
  Name = c("Zoe", "Kai", "Lila", "Ethan", "Leo", "Ezra", "Isla", "Zara", "Maya", "Raja", "Catherine", "Takeshi", "Sven", "Anouk", "Amara"),
  Animal = c("Clownfish", "Panda", "Elephant", "Penguin", "Koala", "Tiger", "Giraffe", "Rabbit", "Cat", "Fox", "Dog", "Otter", "Parrot", "Owl", "Llama"))


full_join(children, animals, by = "Name") |>
  mutate(
    Age = case_when(
      Name == "Catherine" ~ 5,
      Name == "Takeshi" ~ 8,
      Name == "Sven" ~ 8,
      Name == "Anouk" ~ 3,
      Name == "Amara" ~ 11,
      TRUE ~ Age           # Keep everything else as it is.
    ),
    School = case_when(
      Age >= 1 & Age <= 5 ~ "Preschool",
      Age >= 6 & Age <= 9 ~ "Primary school",
      Age >= 10 & Age <= 15 ~ "Middle school",
      TRUE ~ "Highschool"
    )) |>
  group_by(School) |>
  summarise(
    N = n(),
    Mean_Age = mean(Age)
  ) |>
  arrange(N)

```

<div>

**Hint:** Think about how to handle the cases where you **don't** want to change the age.

</div>

You can add labels such as title and subtitle to your plot, as well as rename the x and y axes and color guides by using the `labs()` function.

Create a point ggplot from the `iris` data:

```{r labels-1-solution}
  aes(x = Petal.Length,

      color = Species,
```

### Exercise 17.22: Add labels again

Create a histogram plot from the `starwars` data:

- Remove the missing values.
- Plot the height on the x axis.
- Use gender for coloring the bars.
- Set the number of bins in the geom to 20 and the bar position to dodge.
- Use the minimal theme.
- Add a title and a subtitle to the plot.
- Change the x and y axes labels, as well as the fill.

and the gender on 

```{r labels-2, exercise=TRUE}
# Write your code here

```


```{r}
starwars |>
 filter(!is.na(gender)) |>
 ggplot() +
  aes(x = height, 
      group = gender,
      fill = gender) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, position = position_dodge()) +
  labs(
    x = "Height (cm)",
    y = "Count",
    title = "Starwars characters",
    subtitle = "Character height distribution by gender",
    fill = "Gender") +
  theme_minimal()
```

<div>

<i class="fa-solid fa-circle-info"></i> **Hint:** You can adjust the bar position within the geom as `position = position_dodge()` if you want the bars to be next to each other (as opposed to stacked).

</div>
